the epigenetic regulation of gene activity and its implications for human development, health and disease.
the epigenetic regulation of imprinted genes during oocyte development.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
imprinting of genes in the female germ cell is a dynamic process that occurs over a prolonged period of time.

(1) imprinting of the Snrnp, Igf2, Peg1, Peg3 genes is acquired during oocyte growth; (2) methylation is acquired in a gene-specific manner; and (3) methylation of the repetitive IAPs is also acquired at the same time.
the timing of methylation acquisition of imprinted genes is not uniform and that the timing is related to gene size and location.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
imprint acquisition is a gene-specific process that occurs during oocyte growth and is probably regulated by the accumulation of DNA methyltransferases.
imprinting is not an on-off switch but rather a gradual process.
imprint acquisition occurs in a gene-specific manner, and that this process coincides with the accumulation of de novo DNA methyltransferases in growing oocytes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
methylation of differentially methylated domains (DMDs) occurs asynchronously in the growing oocyte, and the methylation of DMDs is related to oocyte size.
the timing of imprint acquisition varies from gene to gene and is probably related to their developmental functions.
imprinting is not a one-size-fits all process, and that the timing and mechanisms by which imprinting occurs is gene-specific.
